title: My Daily Routine
description: A Sanaa day from the dawn prayer to the late-night series, told in the first person: I wake up, I drink, I go, I chew. Every present-tense form for every person, and the بـ that means 'right now'.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — the learner narrates their own day. Each verb is heard in the first person ('I wake up') before the paradigm is shown; the table comes last, as a summary of what has already been said.
unlock_condition: ≥10/14 on the conjugation fill-in and a recorded one-minute 'my day' with at least six of the verbs
can_do: Describe your ordinary day with eight core verbs
Conjugate the present tense for every person
Ask what someone does every day

grammar.title: The present tense: one verb, every person
grammar.explanation: The person is carried by the beginning of the verb, and sometimes its end. أ- is 'I', تـ is 'you' and 'she', يـ is 'he', نـ is 'we'. Talking to a woman adds -i at the end (تشربي); talking to a group or about a group adds -u (تشربو، يشربو) with no final n. Sanaa still has separate forms for a group of women (تشربين، يشربين) — you will hear them from older speakers, and nobody minds if you use the -u forms instead. Learn one verb this way and you have learned them all.

grammar.title: بـ: right now — and, in Sanaa, increasingly always
grammar.explanation: The plain verb describes what you do in general: أشتغل في مكتب, 'I work in an office'. Put بـ on the front and it means it is happening now: هو بيشتغل, 'he is working (at the moment)'. In today's Sanaa you will hear بـ on habits too, so it is never wrong in a main clause. What stays bare is the verb after 'want', 'must' or 'can': أشتي أنام, 'I want to sleep'. Down south in Aden بـ means the future instead, so a southerner's بأسير is 'I'll go' — a note to file away for now.

examples.english: the kids are studying in the room
I want to go back home
I work in an office in Sanaa

culture.title: The shape of a Sanaa day
culture.note: The day starts with the dawn call to prayer, and many people go straight back to sleep after it. Breakfast is bread with tea, milk tea or a bowl of fatta. The big meal is lunch, around two o'clock — saltah or a rice dish — and everything closes for it. After lunch comes the afternoon lull: the مقيل, when men (and women, separately) sit in the mafraj chewing qat until the sunset prayer. Life starts again after that; dinner is late and light, and the streets and shops are busy until midnight. If you are invited 'in the afternoon', the invitation is to chew.

phrases.english: Will you chew with us this afternoon?
After the dawn prayer I sleep a little

culture.title: Asking about someone's day
culture.note: Asking 'what do you do every day?' is a normal way to get to know someone, and the answer is expected to mention prayer times, since the day is told by them: 'after Fajr', 'before Asr', 'after Maghrib'. Answer the same way and you will sound local at once. Nobody says a clock time when a prayer name will do.

phrases.english: What do you do every day?
I come back home after Asr

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first verb of the day and the first 'I' form: the أ- at the front is you. Yemeni uses صحى/يصحى for waking; you will also hear أقوم, 'I get up'. Not the MSA أستيقظ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person sitting up in bed stretching, early light through a stained-glass window.

example.english: I wake up at dawn every day

vocabulary.video_hint: A morning vlog opening — the vlogger in bed or just up, saying 'I wake up at…'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The model verb for this lesson's table: أشرب، تشرب، يشرب، نشرب. Note the i in the 'you/he/we' forms (tishrab, yishrab) — Sanaa pronounces the prefix vowel clearly.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand lifting a glass of milk tea to the lips, steam rising.

example.english: I drink milk tea in the morning

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone drinking tea or qishr on camera while narrating; the verb said as the glass is raised.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'I' form starts with a long aa (the أ of 'I' plus the أ of the verb). He eats is ياكل, we eat ناكل. The imperative 'eat!' is just كل — you will hear it from every host.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person eating from a shared platter of rice and meat with the right hand.

example.english: I eat lunch at two o'clock

vocabulary.video_hint: A meal on screen with the speaker saying what or when they eat.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa's own word for 'go' is سار/يسير, which in MSA means 'walk'. أروح is heard too and is fine, but أسير marks you as having learned the highland dialect. No preposition is needed before the place: أسير السوق.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man in a zanna and jambiya walking out of a doorway into a sunlit Sanaa lane.

example.english: I go to work at eight

vocabulary.video_hint: The vlogger leaving the house or heading somewhere: 'now I'm going to…'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From the same root as شغل, 'work' (the noun you already know). The 'I' form sounds like ash-TA-ghil; the middle vowel is short. In Sanaa بيشتغل is 'he's working right now'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman at a desk with a laptop and a cup of tea in a small office.

example.english: I work from eight to two

vocabulary.video_hint: Workplace footage with narration; 'ayš tishtaghil?' in street interviews.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A u-verb: أدرس، يدرس (adrus, yidrus). It is also the verb for 'learn' at a class or with a tutor, so 'I study Arabic' is exactly what you will say about this app.
vocabulary.image_scene: A student at a low table with an open Arabic textbook and a notebook.
vocabulary.video_hint: Study or exam-season vlogs; a student explaining their timetable.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Long aa in every form: أنام، ينام، ننام. Also 'go to bed'. The noun النوم, 'sleep', gives you غرفة النوم, 'bedroom', next lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person asleep under a blanket, a lamp switched off beside them.

example.english: I sleep at ten at night

vocabulary.video_hint: Night-routine vlogs; the closing line of a day-in-the-life.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends in ع — feel it in the throat. 'Come back home' takes no preposition: أرجع البيت. The past 'I came back' (رجعت) arrives in Lesson 8.
vocabulary.image_scene: Someone coming in through a front door with shopping bags, greeted by a child.

example.english: I come back home in the afternoon

vocabulary.video_hint: The vlogger arriving back home: 'we're back', 'I come back at…'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The day in Yemen is told by the five prayers, so this verb comes with the prayer names: أصلّي الفجر، أصلّي العصر. Hold the doubled ل. The noun is صلاة.
vocabulary.image_scene: Rows of men praying in a whitewashed Sanaa mosque, dawn light.

example.english: I pray the dawn prayer at the mosque

vocabulary.video_hint: The call to prayer or a mosque in a vlog; 'after we pray…' in narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Watching TV, a series or a match. Many Yemenis simply say أشوف ('I see') for the same thing — both are accepted. Doubled ر in the middle.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family on floor cushions watching a Ramadan series on a wall-mounted TV.

example.english: I watch a series at night

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone in front of a TV or phone screen; reactions to a series or match.

vocabulary.teaching_note: كل + a singular noun = 'every'. كل يوم جمعة is 'every Friday'. It usually sits at the end of the sentence.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wall calendar with every day ticked in green.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any routine narration — 'every day I…' — is the anchor for this phrase.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said with the -an ending kept, unlike most classical endings. Goes at the front or straight after the subject. غالباً, 'mostly', is the common alternative.
vocabulary.image_scene: A clock at two o'clock and a plate of saltah on a table, repeated three times across the frame.

example.english: I usually have lunch at two

vocabulary.video_hint: 'Usually I…' in a routine or Q&A video.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A Sanaa verb from صباح, 'morning'. Two emphatic letters in a row (ص then ط) — say them low and full. Breakfast itself is الصبوح or الفطور.
vocabulary.image_scene: A breakfast spread: flatbread, a bowl of beans, a glass of tea with milk.

example.english: I have bread and tea for breakfast

vocabulary.video_hint: Breakfast vlogs and street-food mornings: fuul, fatta, tea.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From الغدا, 'lunch', the main meal. 'Have lunch with us' — تغدّى معنا — is the most common invitation you will hear. Doubled د.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family seated on the floor around a large tray of saltah and bread.
vocabulary.video_hint: Lunch scenes; the host saying 'come and have lunch'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'I store' — the leaves are kept in the cheek for hours. The verb for the afternoon session, which structures the second half of a Yemeni day. Doubled ز.
vocabulary.image_scene: Men reclining on cushions in a bright mafraj, a bundle of green qat leaves in front of each.

example.english: After lunch I chew qat with friends

vocabulary.video_hint: A qat session filmed in a mafraj; the qat market; 'let's go chew'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first fixed point of the day and the way people say 'very early'. 'At dawn' needs no preposition: أصحى الفجر. The ج is a full j in Sanaa.
vocabulary.image_scene: Sanaa's tower houses against a pale pink dawn sky, a minaret lit up.
vocabulary.video_hint: The dawn call to prayer over Sanaa; 'after Fajr' in a routine.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The afternoon is named after its prayer. In Yemen it is qat time: 'I'll see you in the afternoon' means at the session. The ع and ص together are a workout — go slowly.
vocabulary.image_scene: Late-afternoon golden light on a Sanaa street, shops reopening.

example.english: In the afternoon everyone is at the qat session

vocabulary.video_hint: Afternoon footage; 'this afternoon' in a plan or invitation.

dialogue.speaker: Bilqis
dialogue.arabic: ايش تعمل كل يوم يا صلاح؟
dialogue.transliteration: aysh tiʿmal kull yawm ya ṣalaaḥ?
dialogue.english: What do you do every day, Salah?

dialogue.speaker: Salah
dialogue.english: I wake up at dawn, pray, then have breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: Bilqis
dialogue.english: And what time do you go to work?

dialogue.speaker: Salah
dialogue.arabic: الساعة ثمان. أشتغل لين الساعة ثنتين وأرجع أتغدى.
dialogue.transliteration: is-saaʿa thamaan. ashtaghil layn is-saaʿa thintayn w-arjaʿ atghadda.
dialogue.english: At eight. I work until two and come back for lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Salah
dialogue.arabic: العصر عادةً أخزّن مع الأصحاب، وبالليل أتفرج مسلسل وأنام.
dialogue.transliteration: il-ʿaṣr ʿaadatan akhazzin maʿ il-aṣḥaab, w-bil-layl atfarraj musalsal w-anaam.
dialogue.english: In the afternoon I usually chew qat with friends, and at night I watch a series and sleep.

sound_spotlight.explanation: The 'right now' prefix and the 'he' prefix glide together into one syllable, biy-. Don't insert a pause between them.
Sanaa speech squeezes unstressed short vowels. In fast speech the a of tishrabi almost disappears; listen for the consonants and the stressed syllable.
Two emphatic consonants back to back. The whole word sits low in the mouth; the a vowels sound almost like o.

lesson_sequence.detail: Salah's day plays through as a picture story: eight cards, each with the 'I' form of a verb auto-playing, Arabic large, no English.
Same eight cards with English shown; then the time words (كل يوم، عادةً، الفجر، العصر) placed on a clock face.
Listen to a form (تشربي، يدرس، نخزّن) and tap the person it belongs to. The table appears only after this.
Pairs of sentences with and without بـ; tap 'right now' or 'in general'.
Drag the verbs onto a timeline from الفجر to بالليل and hear the sentence the app builds for each.
Record 'my day' in six sentences; the app checks the verbs it hears against the checklist.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tonight, before you sleep, say your day in Arabic in your head: أصحى… أشرب… أسير… أرجع… أنام.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Activates the 'I' forms in order.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask a Yemeni friend or your tutor: ايش تعمل كل يوم؟ — and listen for which prayer names they use as clock times.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Activates the question and the prayer-name time words.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you see someone doing something, say it with بـ: هو بيشرب، هي بتدرس.
real_world_prompts.context: Observation prompt for the 'right now' prefix.

video_needs.scene: A day-in-the-life vlog narrated in the first person: waking, tea, going to work, the two o'clock lunch, the afternoon qat session, the evening series.
